This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# deadnix

Scan `.nix` files for dead code (unused variable bindings).

## Usage with Github Actions

See [deadnix-action](https://github.com/astro/deadnix-action)


## Usage with Nix Flakes

### Help

```console
nix run github:astro/deadnix -- --help
Find dead code in .nix files

Usage: deadnix [OPTIONS] [FILE_PATHS]...

Arguments:
  [FILE_PATHS]...  .nix files, or directories with .nix files inside [default: .]

Options:
  -l, --no-lambda-arg                  Don't check lambda parameter arguments
  -L, --no-lambda-pattern-names        Don't check lambda attrset pattern names (don't break nixpkgs callPackage)
  -_, --no-underscore                  Don't check any bindings that start with a _
  -q, --quiet                          Don't print dead code report
  -e, --edit                           Remove unused code and write to source file
  -h, --hidden                         Recurse into hidden subdirectories and process hidden .*.nix files
      --help
  -f, --fail                           Exit with 1 if unused code has been found
  -o, --output-format <OUTPUT_FORMAT>  Output format to use [default: human-readable] [possible values: human-readable, json]
      --exclude <EXCLUDES>...          Files to exclude from analysis
  -V, --version                        Print version
```

Reports contain ANSI color escape codes unless the
[`$NO_COLOR`](https://no-color.org/) environment variable is set.

The `--exclude` parameter accepts multiple paths. Separate them with
`--` to pass `[FILE_PATHS]...`.

### Scan for unused code

```console
nix run github:astro/deadnix example.nix
Warning: Unused declarations were found.
    ╭─[example.nix:1:1]
  1 │unusedArgs@{ unusedArg, usedArg, ... }:
    ·     │           ╰───── Unused lambda pattern: unusedArg
    ·     ╰───────────────── Unused lambda pattern: unusedArgs
  3 │  inherit (builtins) unused_inherit;
    ·                            ╰─────── Unused let binding: unused_inherit
  5 │  unused = "fnord";
    ·     ╰─── Unused let binding: unused
 10 │  shadowed = 42;
    ·      ╰──── Unused let binding: shadowed
 11 │  _unused = unused: false;
    ·     │         ╰─── Unused lambda argument: unused
    ·     ╰───────────── Unused let binding: _unused
 13 │  x = { unusedArg2, x ? args.y, ... }@args: used1 + x;
    ·             ╰───── Unused lambda pattern: unusedArg2
```


### Remove unused code automatically

**Do commit** your changes into version control **before!**

```console
nix run github:astro/deadnix -- -eq test.nix
```

## Usage with [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/)

Add the following to your project's `.pre-commit-config.yaml`:
```yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astro/deadnix
    rev: ID # frozen: VERSION
    hooks:
      - id: deadnix
        #args: [--edit] # Uncomment to automatically modify files
        stages: [commit]
```

Replace `ID` and `VERSION` above with the relevant version tag and
commit ID for reference, for example:

```yaml
rev: da39a3ee5e6b4b0d3255bfef95601890afd80709  # frozen: v1.2.3
```

## Behavior

### Renaming of all unused to lambda args to start with `_`

If you disfavor marking them as unused, use option
`-l`/`--no-lambda-arg`.


### nixpkgs `callPackages` with multiple imports

`callPackages` guesses the packages to inject by the names of a
packages' lambda attrset pattern names. Some packages alias these with
`@args` to pass them to another `import ...nix args`.

As the used args are only named in the imported file they will be
recognized as dead in the package source file that is imported by
`callPackage`, rendering it unable to guess the dependencies to call
the packages with.

Use option `-L`/`--no-lambda-pattern-names` in this case.


### Skipping reports for certain declarations

As of 1.1.0 deadnix supports the following pragma to skip check of
bindings in the following line:

```nix
# deadnix: skip
```


## What if the produced reports are wrong?

Please open an issue. Do not forget to include the `.nix` code that
produces incorrect results.

# Quick test to see with understanding: outer variable considered unused if with attribute of same name exists and is used, but outer shadowed?

# Similarly, let x=1; y=2; in with { y=3; }; x => y unused (outer y shadowed, not used), x used (outer). That matches: outer y unused because with's y shadows but body doesn't use y, it uses x. Outer y unused. With's y unused? But deadnix only checks let and lambda, not with's internal bindings, so with's bindings are not checked as unused.
# So implementation of 'with': when we enter with, we need to understand that variables in its namespace (if we can resolve statically) may shadow outer variables, causing outer to be unused.

# Need to know when with scope is static set { ... } - then we know which names it provides.
# If with set contains e.g., y, then any reference to y inside with body could be resolved to with's y, not outer.
# How does deadnix decide? It seems:
# - If with set is { y=3 } and body uses y, outer y considered unused (shadowed). That suggests if with set provides name, it shadows outer.
# - If with set is { y=3 } and body uses x, outer y unused, outer x considered used (since x not in with set, must come from outer).
# - If with set is {} empty, then nothing shadowed, outer variables used normally.

# What about with set { z=3 } and body uses z: then body z comes from with, outer not needed, outer unused (as seen: let x=1; y=2; in with { z=3; }; z => both outer unused, because z from with).

# What about with set { z=y } where y refers to outer? Then y is used inside with set definition. Example: let x=1; y=2; in with { z=y; }; z => earlier test said x unused, y used? Let's check: we had let x=1; y=2; in with { z=y; }; z => result: x unused. That means y is considered used because with's set uses y. Indeed, the set's values may reference outer variables.

# So we need to model: with pushes a dynamic scope that may provide unknown names. But when with set is a static attrset literal { ... }, we know which names it defines, and we can treat those names as shadowing outer for the body.
# Also the with set's own values are evaluated not in with scope? Actually with { y=x; } - does y's default use outer x? Yes. So the set's definitions should be evaluated in outer scope, not including with's own shadowing? Example: let x=1; in with { y=x; }; y => no unused, x used inside with set. So set's values use outer scope.
# What about with set that contains its own internal references? e.g., with { a=1; b=a; }: does b's a refer to outer or to a from same set? In attrset, normally a=1; b=a; means b refers to a inside set (if rec? Actually attrset non-rec: b=a would refer to outer a, not previous a, unless rec. But with set that is { a=1; b=a; } - is that b=a where a is from same set? In nix, attrset is non-rec by default unless rec. So b=a would not see a from same set unless rec. However with { a=1; b=a; } - b's a might be from outer? Need to check how deadnix handles attrset internal references.

# Check attrset internal ref handling earlier: let a=1; in { a=1; b=a; } => we saw earlier test for { a=1; b=a; } with outer a=1: outer a was considered unused? Let's re-run.

PY
python3 /tmp/runner.py
"}

# deadnix

Scan `.nix` files for dead code (unused variable bindings).

## Usage with Github Actions

See [deadnix-action](https://github.com/astro/deadnix-action)


## Usage with Nix Flakes

### Help

```console
nix run github:astro/deadnix -- --help
Find dead code in .nix files

Usage: deadnix [OPTIONS] [FILE_PATHS]...

Arguments:
  [FILE_PATHS]...  .nix files, or directories with .nix files inside [default: .]

Options:
  -l, --no-lambda-arg                  Don't check lambda parameter arguments
  -L, --no-lambda-pattern-names        Don't check lambda attrset pattern names (don't break nixpkgs callPackage)
  -_, --no-underscore                  Don't check any bindings that start with a _
  -q, --quiet                          Don't print dead code report
  -e, --edit                           Remove unused code and write to source file
  -h, --hidden                         Recurse into hidden subdirectories and process hidden .*.nix files
      --help
  -f, --fail                           Exit with 1 if unused code has been found
  -o, --output-format <OUTPUT_FORMAT>  Output format to use [default: human-readable] [possible values: human-readable, json]
      --exclude <EXCLUDES>...          Files to exclude from analysis
  -V, --version                        Print version
```

Reports contain ANSI color escape codes unless the
[`$NO_COLOR`](https://no-color.org/) environment variable is set.

The `--exclude` parameter accepts multiple paths. Separate them with
`--` to pass `[FILE_PATHS]...`.

# Summary of with handling observed:
# - with expr; body
#   expr evaluated in outer scope (usages in expr count as usage of outer)
#   body evaluated in a scope where:
#     if expr is a set literal { ... } (including possibly empty), then its keys shadow outer names.
#       So if body uses name that is key in expr, outer binding with same name is NOT considered used (shadowed).
#       If body uses name not in expr keys, then outer binding with that name IS considered used (if exists).
#       If body uses name that is not in outer nor in expr keys, then it's unknown (maybe from somewhere else), but for dead detection we don't care.
#   If expr is NOT a set literal (variable, etc.), then we cannot know its keys. In that case, for any body usage, we conservatively assume it could be from outer OR from with. So we should consider outer as used if body contains that name? From earlier: with a; b where outer has b, and with arg is unknown, outer b not reported unused (so considered used). That suggests for unknown with, body name usages are considered as possibly using outer, so outer considered used.
#   Also, for unknown with, if body uses name not in outer, we don't report outer unused for other names. For example, let a=1; b=2; in with a; c => outer b reported unused (because c does not match b). So only names that appear in body are considered used.
#   So algorithm for unknown with: body usages still count as using outer if name matches, i.e., same as normal, but additionally, any body usage does NOT prevent outer from being considered used due to shadowing, because we don't know if with provides that name. So we treat unknown with as NOT shadowing any outer names.
#   Thus:
#     known set literal: shadow set = keys of set
#     unknown: shadow set = empty (no shadowing)
#   Then body scope: if shadow set non-empty, any outer binding whose name is in shadow set and used only in body where that name appears, should NOT be considered used via body (since shadowed). But if that outer is also used elsewhere (e.g., in expr or in other outer bindings that are used), it could still be used.

        self.type=type_
        self.text=text
        self.line=line
        self.col=col
        self.end_line=end_line
        self.end_col=end_col
        self.offset=offset
        self.end_offset=end_offset
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Token({self.type},{self.text!r},{self.line}:{self.col})"

    'let':'LET',
    'in':'IN',
    'inherit':'INHERIT',
    'rec':'REC',
    'with':'WITH',
    'if':'IF',
    'then':'THEN',
    'else':'ELSE',
    'assert':'ASSERT',
    'or':'OR_KW',
}

    skip_lines = set()

        nonlocal line, col, offset, i
        # text may contain newlines

                line+=1
                col=1
            else:
                col+=1
            offset+=1
            i+=1

    # For simplicity, implement iterative with state stack
    # State: ('CODE',) or ('STRING_DQ', start_line, start_col, start_offset, content_start) or ('IND_STRING', ...)
    # Also need to handle ${ interpolation: when inside STRING, encountering "${" we push STRING and enter CODE for interpolation, expecting to find matching "}" .
    # But interpolation expression itself can contain strings that contain interpolations, etc., so we need stack.

    # We'll use a stack of states, each state is dict with type and other info
    # Initial state CODE
    state_stack = [{'type':'CODE'}]

    # We'll when in CODE, handle tokens as before, but when we encounter " we enter STRING_DQ.

                for _ in text:

    def __init__(self, type_, text, line, col, end_line, end_col, offset, end_offset):

        self.col=col
        self.end_line=end_line
        self.end_col=end_col
        self.offset=offset
        self.end_offset=end_offset

        return f"Token({self.type},{self.text!r},{self.line}:{self.col})"

# deadnix

Scan `.nix` files for dead code (unused variable bindings).

## Usage with Github Actions

See [deadnix-action](https://github.com/astro/deadnix-action)


## Usage with Nix Flakes

### Help

```console
nix run github:astro/deadnix -- --help
Find dead code in .nix files

Usage: deadnix [OPTIONS] [FILE_PATHS]...

Arguments:
  [FILE_PATHS]...  .nix files, or directories with .nix files inside [default: .]

Options:
  -l, --no-lambda-arg                  Don't check lambda parameter arguments
  -L, --no-lambda-pattern-names        Don't check lambda attrset pattern names (don't break nixpkgs callPackage)
  -_, --no-underscore                  Don't check any bindings that start with a _
  -q, --quiet                          Don't print dead code report
  -e, --edit                           Remove unused code and write to source file
  -h, --hidden                         Recurse into hidden subdirectories and process hidden .*.nix files
      --help
  -f, --fail                           Exit with 1 if unused code has been found
  -o, --output-format <OUTPUT_FORMAT>  Output format to use [default: human-readable] [possible values: human-readable, json]
      --exclude <EXCLUDES>...          Files to exclude from analysis
  -V, --version                        Print version
```

Reports contain ANSI color escape codes unless the
[`$NO_COLOR`](https://no-color.org/) environment variable is set.

The `--exclude` parameter accepts multiple paths. Separate them with
`--` to pass `[FILE_PATHS]...`.

### Scan for unused code

nix run github:astro/deadnix example.nix
Warning: Unused declarations were found.
    ╭─[example.nix:1:1]
  1 │unusedArgs@{ unusedArg, usedArg, ... }:

So it will not consume comma, and will treat entry x as complete, then continue loop: next token after x is EQ, not COMMA, not ELLIPSIS, not IDENT, not R_BRACE, so it will go to self.pos+=1 (skip token).
